extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of American public administration and local government
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and describing the institutional features, functions, and legal/political practices of American local and municipal governments, including comparative notes and charter examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of local government (police, sanitation, poor relief, education)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general functions of local government include police, sanitation, poor relief, and education; education 'is indeed almost the only matter which has been deemed to demand a special body to handle it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that police, sanitation, and poor relief are 'simpler and less costly than in England' and that it has been easier in the U.S. 'to vest the management of all in the same local authority.' Education is frequently detached to a separate body (Board of Education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of political party influence in rural local government
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of political party permeation varies greatly — county officials are 'apt to be chosen on political lines,' whereas 'in the township and rural school district party spirit is much less active.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains causes (population character, intensity of party feeling, overlap with election districts), effects (party 'county ticket' intrudes national politics, makes it harder for non-professional politicians to enter administration), and counterexamples (township offices often unpaid; personal merits better known).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and non-overlap of local divisions and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: In each State the local system is 'eminently simple' compared with pre-1888 rural England: 'few local divisions, few authorities; the divisions and authorities rarely overlap.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity reduces administrative cost and duplication; absence of an intermediate third local area (like English Rural Districts) noted as characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated tax-levying and collection method
rubrics_metrics.description: In most States a citizen 'pays at the same time, to the same officer, upon the same paper of demand, all his local taxes, and not only these, but also his State tax.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: saves expense (State leans on local officials), spares taxpayer repeated calls upon the cheque-book; some city taxes may be paid separately and there are options (half-yearly/quarterly) and discounts for advance payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of local government responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The sphere of local government 'is in America unusually wide' and 'widest in ... New England and the North-West.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although fewer functions may be needed compared to England, practical competence of local authorities is deemed sufficient to undertake new functions the State may entrust to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township/town-meeting as preferred local unit
rubrics_metrics.description: The township with its popular primary assembly (town-meeting) 'has been the best. It is the cheapest and the most efficient; it is the most educative to the citizens who bear a part in it. The town-meeting has been not only the source but the school of democracy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that the township unit 'needs...to be supplemented...by that of the county' in some respects; the mixed Middle States system has produced a more perfect type by combining attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical composition of city government
rubrics_metrics.description: Most larger cities have: a mayor (head of the executive, elected directly), certain executive officers or boards (some elected, some appointed), a legislature (usually two chambers but sometimes one), and judges (elected or appointed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains correspondences to State government (mayor ~ Governor, aldermen/common council ~ legislature) and variation among cities; charter and state law determine exact form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayoral powers, term, and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The mayor holds office (commonly 2–4 years), often directly elected by the whole city, usually not a member of the city legislature, has a veto on ordinances (overridable by two-thirds), often appoints department heads, may be made responsible for departments and liable to impeachment, and has duties to 'provide for the public peace, to quell riots, and, if necessary, to call out the militia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variations: some cities prohibit re-eligibility; salary varies (example: New York up to $15,000); in some cities mayor sits in the legislature (Chicago, San Francisco); mayoral discretion in law enforcement (e.g., enforcement of Sunday Closing Acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative departments and fragmentation risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration is carried on by a number of departments, sometimes under one head, sometimes as boards/commissions; 'chief executive officers have been disconnected from one another' and communicate more with legislative committees than with the legislature as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This disconnection leads to problems: committees 'job it,' secrecy, lack of coordination, and disconnecting departments from one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of education administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is 'generally treated as a distinct matter' and committed to a Board of Education whose members are separately elected or appointed, levy a separate tax, and have their own executive staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although sometimes the city legislature appoints a Board of Education (Baltimore), detaching education from politics is desirable; where education is 'within politics' results can be unfavorable to teacher independence and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: City legislative organization and committee system
rubrics_metrics.description: City legislatures commonly consist of one chamber in small cities and sometimes two in large ones (Board of Aldermen and Common Council); members are generally elected by wards, with the upper house sometimes elected by districts or on a 'general ticket.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Councils usually serve short terms (one or two years for common council), often unpaid in small cities; committees are used to manage business but have evils of secrecy and irresponsibility and can disconnect departments from one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and politicization of municipal judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: City judges are usually elected by citizens for various terms, though sometimes appointed by the State or mayor; appointment methods can be used to reserve judicial offices from local majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New Haven — county delegation in the State legislature nominates judges, producing partisan selection; the text argues for the practicalities of existing arrangements given political morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of municipal elections and effects on voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal elections often coincide with State or Federal elections to save expense, but this 'bewilders the voter' and encourages straight-ticket voting; there is a tendency to fix municipal elections on different dates so citizens may give undistracted, non-partisan thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off: holding municipal elections with state elections may increase turnout and choice, but may also socialize voting on party lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of party loyalty and straight-ticket voting
rubrics_metrics.description: The disposition to run and vote by party is 'practically universal' and many voters give 'little thought to the personal qualifications' of municipal candidates, voting the 'straight ticket.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When both parties nominate questionable men, non-partisan or 'citizens' tickets' may be run by combinations of respectable men; sometimes they succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission plan of municipal government
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission plan: a small board of commissioners (example: Galveston five commissioners; Des Moines four commissioners plus mayor) elected at large, each assigned a department; the Commission passes ordinances, votes the budget, gives contracts, makes principal appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported outcomes: marked improvements in municipal work, reduction of floating debt, municipal ownership of utilities; features include recall (one-fourth of voters can demand) and referendum for franchises/ordinances; at-large elections can reduce party influence but sometimes produce 'odd results.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of city functions into three groups
rubrics_metrics.description: City functions are distributed into three groups: (a) delegated by the State (coercive powers, licences, enforcement), (b) matters under general laws but locally charged (education, care of the poor), and (c) business-like services (paving, drains, water, light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first two make the city a political entity; the third is likened to a business corporation in which taxpayers are shareholders; all three are dealt with alike by American legislation though education is usually detached and police sometimes placed under separate control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation/independence of police and regulatory control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of the police has sometimes been withheld from city government and conferred upon separate boards (e.g., Boston police board appointed by State governor and council), often with statutory direction to represent both political parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to take departments 'out of politics'; examples include New York's unwritten practice of bipartisan police commissioners and Boston's 1885 statute creating a state-appointed board for police and liquor licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal taxation practice and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes in cities are levied on personal as well as real property and are usually collected with county and State taxes; both real and personal property are often assessed well below true value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: higher taxes in larger cities lead to migration of rich men to suburbs (tax flight), shrinking civic participation of wealthy residents, and an increased tax burden on those who remain; assessors tend to minimize city burden on their own communities but are checked by county and State Boards of Equalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limits on municipal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: American municipal governments are subject to three general rules: they have no powers other than those conferred by the State, they cannot delegate their powers, and their legislation and action is subject to the U.S. Constitution as well as the Constitution and statutes of their State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constraints frame the legal authority and limits of city governments and explain why city charters and state laws are decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charter-level electoral and appointment rules (Boston example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boston (charter 1909): mayoral nominations only by petitions signed by at least 5,000 qualified voters on official forms, signatures scrutinized by Election Commissioners; candidates placed on non‑partisan ballots in order determined by lot; municipal election date and fiscal year fixed; mayoral recall possible at mid-term requiring majority of total enrolled votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional charter rules: mayor elected for four years with recall at two years; mayor appoints heads of departments (appointments require certificate from State Civil Service Commission of qualifications); mayoral removals require detailed specific reasons; salary example given ($10,000). These are examples of how charters can structure candidate access, ballot form, appointment oversight, and recall thresholds.
